newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican tequila war ends, blockade lifted.
newsitem.headline: Mexican tequila war ends, blockade lifted.

text.p: Mexican farmers on Wednesday lifted a 21-day blockade of 11 top tequila producers, ending a war that producers said had threatened supplies of the powerful liquor around the world.

The farmers, members of a militant debtors movement called El Barzon, ended their blockade after they agreed with industrialists on a suitable price for agave cactus, one of the hard-to-grow raw materials of tequila.

In a communique, the state government said both sides had agreed on a price of 650 pesos ($85) per ton of agave between Oct. 9 and Nov. 30, up from 500 pesos before the blockade. The price was set to go steadily higher afterward.

The blockade had thrown the town of Tequila into chaos, with no trucks carrying agave or sugar allowed to enter or leave since Sept. 19. This week, the producers -- some big name exporters -- warned of supplies running out at home and abroad.
The protesters said they were forced to take action because of low prices paid for agave, which takes from eight to 10 years to grow.
Besides the 30 percent immediate increase, both sides also agreed on agave prices of 800 pesos a ton from Dec. 1 to Jan. 31, 1997 and 850 pesos from Feb. 1997 onwards.
